questions.question: How the methodical doubt of Descartes contributed to the development of scientific thinking
questions.solution_html:
• Descartes' methodical doubt- I think, therefore I am- promoting scepticism as a
  • tool for uncovering the truth- doubting everything that could be doubted
  • establishes a foundation of specific knowledge based solely on reason- shifted
  • the focus of inquiry from reliance on tradition or authority to individual rational
  • investigation- encouraged future scientists to question assumptions, emphasise
  • empirical evidence, and adopt a systematic approach to discovering knowledge
  • Descartes helped shape the scientific method, prioritising doubt
  • experimentation, and evidence-based conclusions.
  • (Aligns with CO1: Understand the epistemological developments in modern
  • science.)

questions.question: What is the theory of natural selection
questions.solution_html:
• Charles Darwin- theory of natural selection-organisms better suited to their
  • environment are more likely to survive and reproduce- advantageous traits to
  • future generations- tiny changes accumulate leading to the evolution of new
  • species- natural selection operates on variation within populations, with
  • environmental pressures determining favourable characteristics- forms the
  • cornerstone of evolutionary biology and provides a scientific explanation for the
  • diversity of life on Earth.
  • (Aligns with CO2: Analyse the non-European roots of scientific traditions.)
questions.final_answer: (Aligns with CO2: Analyse the non-European roots of scientific traditions.)

questions.question: Explain the process of institutionalization of scientific practice in Europe
questions.solution_html:
• The institutionalisation of scientific practice in Europe- Renaissance and
  • Enlightenment- scientific inquiry shifted from primarily pursuing individuals or
  • small groups to becoming a more formalised and institutionalised activity
  • establishment of scientific societies like the Royal Society of London in 1660
  • platforms for collaboration, knowledge sharing, and the standardisation of
  • scientific methods- Universities - incorporating science into their curricula
  • institutionalisation helped legitimise science as a professional discipline and
  • facilitated its rapid advancement.
  • (Aligns with CO1: Understand the epistemological, methodological, and
  • institutional developments in modern science.)

questions.question: Survey the material milieu of the development of science in Arab world
questions.solution_html:
• The material milieu of science in the Arab world during its Golden Age (8th to

  • like mathematics, astronomy, medicine, and chemistry- role of trade, wealth
  • from the empire, and a network of scholars in the growth of scientific inquiry.
  • (Aligns with CO2: Analyse the non-European roots of scientific traditions.)

questions.question: Examine the influence of post modernism in the theory and knowledge of scientific practice
questions.solution_html:
• Postmodernism- challenging the idea of objective, universal truths in science
  • scientific knowledge is socially constructed and shaped by cultural, political, and
  • historical contexts - critiques the traditional view of science as an impartial
  • pursuit of truth, emphasising instead that power dynamics, ideologies, and the
  • interests of dominant groups influence scientific practices- focus on the
  • subjectivity involved in scientific inquiry, calling for more inclusive and diverse
  • perspectives in scientific research- rethinking of scientific authority and a more
  • critical view of the assumptions underlying scientific methodologies.
  • (Aligns with CO3: Assess how science viewed social structures and institutions
  • in the Western world and colonies.)
questions.final_answer: in the Western world and colonies.)

questions.question: Explain the reasons for the lack of representation of women and gender / minorities in scientific research and profession
questions.solution_html:
• gender minorities in scientific research and profession / – 
  • Professionalization: As science became a paid profession, women were

  • (salonnieres) were vilified as chaotic and neglectful of domestic duties.
  • Public vs. Private: Women were confined to the private/domestic sphere
  • rendering their "amateur" work unscientific.

questions.question: Analyze the development of scientific knowledge in Chinese society in / the premodern times
questions.solution_html:
• Analyze the development of scientific knowledge in Chinese society in the
  • premodern times - / - Joseph Needham: His work ("Science and
  • Civilization in China") debunked the myth that China contributed little to science
  • proving they were ahead of the West Pre-Renaissance - Paper & Printing: Paper
  • was invented by Cai Lun (105 CE). Woodblock printing was followed by movable
  • type in the 10th century. -Gunpowder: Discovered accidentally by Taoist
  • alchemists (charcoal, Sulphur, saltpeter). Weaponized into bombs and barrel
  • guns by 1000–1120 CE.- Porcelain: Developed during the Han dynasty; reached
  • artistic peaks in the Ming dynasty and exported to Europe. - Magnetism: Used
  • Earth's magnetic field for navigation and understood magnetic
  • declination long before the West. - Maritime: Constructed the Grand Canal (1,776
  • km). Invented the sternpost rudder and paddle-wheel boats - Iron & Steel
  • Developed double-acting piston bellows and steel production
  • via carbonation (6th century) - Mechanics: Invented the stirrup, wheelbarrow
  • efficient horse harness, and mechanisms to convert reciprocating motion to
  • rotary motion - Mathematics: Used a decimal place-value system (bamboo rods)
  • and sliding calipers, Liu Hui edited "The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art."
  • Calculated Pi (π) to seven decimal places nine centuries before Europe.-) to seven decimal places nine centuries before Europe.
  • Astronomy: Shi Shen (4th century BCE) created a star catalogue, Recorded the
  • first solar eclipse (1361 BCE), sunspots (28 BCE), and supernova. Built complex
  • Armillary Spheres and hydromechanical clocks (e.g., Kaifeng Tower, 1088 CE).
questions.final_answer: Armillary Spheres and hydromechanical clocks (e.g., Kaifeng Tower, 1088 CE)

questions.question: Critically examine various aspects associated with the Eurocentric / discourses on modern science
questions.solution_html:
• Critically examine various aspects associated with the Eurocentric discourses
  • on modern science - / - The critique of Eurocentrism argues that the
  • "Scientific Revolution" was not a unique European event but a synthesis of global
  • knowledge that erased Islamic, Indian, and Chinese contributions - The
  • "Universal" Trap: Western science is elevated as the sole objective truth, while
  • non-Western systems are dismissed as "ethnoscience" or folklore -Historical
  • Appropriation: Many "Western" breakthroughs have unacknowledged Eastern
  • roots. For instance, the Copernican model utilized Persian mathematics (Tusi)
  • and the "scientific method" was practiced by Ibn al-Haytham centuries before
  • Galileo - "Standard" medical data is overwhelmingly based on European genetics
  • causing treatments to fail for non-white populations, while "helicopter research"
  • exploits Global South resources without credit – Eurocentrism a colonial project
  • still working to establish the European intellectual dominance of the world and
  • establish non-European inferiority.
